sections.h2: Which Carteret County office handles property tax?
sections.html:
The Carteret County Tax Administration office handles it, and in this county one office combines the tax assessor and the tax collector under an appointed Tax Administrator. The county commissioners make that appointment, and the administrator also answers to the state Department of Revenue and the Property Tax Commission on how the law is applied.

The main office is on the first floor of the Administration Building at 302 Courthouse Square, Beaufort, NC 28516, and a Western Office sits at 701 Cedar Point Blvd., Cedar Point, NC 28584. Both are open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., excluding holidays, and the office phone is 252-728-8485. The office is also the staff liaison to the Board of Equalization and Review.

Its stated job covers appraisal, assessment, billing and collection of tax on real, business and personal property, plus keeping the records the state Department of Revenue asks for. If you are selling, this is the office that can tell you what is owed on the parcel and whether any relief claim is on file.

sections.h2: When are Carteret County property taxes due?
sections.html:
They are due September 1 and can be paid without interest through January 5 of the next year. After that the county adds 2% in January and 0.75% for each month the balance stays open.

For fiscal year 2026-27 the county tax rate is 22.5 cents per $100 of assessed value, according to the county's August 2026 release. Real and personal property are billed separately, and owners in Beaufort, Bogue, Cape Carteret, Cedar Point, Emerald Isle, Morehead City and Peletier receive one bill that includes both county and municipal tax. Mailed payments count as received on the postmark date.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Carteret County assessed value?
sections.html:
File the Real Property Appeal Form with the Tax Administration Office by the deadline on your value notice. The county's reappraisal page says the appeal must be received no later than 30 days from the date of the notice, and that appeals can address value only, never the tax rate or the bill.

The county's last general reappraisal used a January 1, 2025 market value, and its notice tells owners to compare their property's characteristics and comparable sales against what was used. State law presumes the assessor acted in good faith, so the owner has to show the value is wrong. Bring sales of similar nearby homes, photos of damage and repair estimates.

  • First level: the Board of Equalization and Review, made up of nine county residents including two alternates. It mails a Notice of Decision within 30 days of its meeting.
  • Second level: the state Property Tax Commission, with 30 days from that notice to file. Appeals are typically heard in Raleigh, and legal representation may be needed.
  • Third level: the North Carolina Court of Appeals, only on a question of law, and then the state Supreme Court.

For personal property such as boats, aircraft, mobile homes and business equipment, the clock is 30 days from the date printed on the annual bill, and the county arranges a conference before a final decision. The county says a ruling can lower, raise or keep the value and applies only from that year forward. Statewide, G.S. 105-290 sets the 30-day window to reach the Property Tax Commission.

sections.h2: What property tax relief can a Carteret County owner claim?
sections.html:
Three state programs may reduce the bill, and each owner can use only one of them. They are the elderly or disabled exclusion, the disabled veteran exclusion and the circuit breaker deferral, all filed with the county tax office rather than the state.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: the greater of $25,000 or 50% of the home's appraised value, for owners at least 65 or totally and permanently disabled with income at or under the limit. The 2026 income limit printed by the Department of Revenue is $38,800.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: the first $45,000 of appraised value, with no age or income limit printed on the state form.
  • Circuit breaker: tax capped at 4.0% of income, or 5.0% when income is over the limit and up to 150% of it, which is $58,200 for 2026. Owners must have lived in the home as a permanent residence for five years.

Applications go on Form AV-9. The state form says to file during the listing period, and the county must accept applications through June 1 before the tax year. The circuit breaker needs a new application every year, and the deferred tax is a lien that comes due for the preceding three years if the owner sells, dies or stops living there. Carteret County's delinquent tax page points seniors, disabled owners and qualifying veterans to its relief programs. Read the statutes at G.S. 105-277.1, 105-277.1B and 105-277.1C.

sections.h2: How can I pay a Carteret County tax bill?
sections.html:
You can pay online, by phone, by mail or in person. The county's taxpayer portal takes credit and debit cards, eCheck and PayPal, and the phone line is 1-888-544-9433 for card payments with a copy of the bill in hand.

  • By mail: make the check payable to County of Carteret and send it to PO Box 96264, Charlotte, NC 28296-6264.
  • In person: Beaufort or Cedar Point, with cash, check, money order or card.
  • Drop box: at the courthouse entrance, no cash, processed the next business day.

Fees apply to cards. The county's payment options page lists a flat $1.50 for an electronic check and 2.50% plus $0.30 per transaction for credit cards. Partial payments in any amount are allowed online, but the full balance must be in before delinquency, and the county's news release says the phone line does not take partial amounts. If you cannot pay in full, the county offers a hardship payment arrangement through an application. It does not stop interest, but it may reduce the chance of garnishment or foreclosure.

sections.h2: What happens when Carteret County taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
The lien on the parcel stays, interest keeps growing, and the county can use enforcement tools. Under G.S. 105-355 the lien attaches as of the listing date, with penalties, interest and costs added to it.

The county lists wage and bank garnishment, state income tax refund setoff, setoff against lottery winnings, attachment of rent, seizure and sale of personal property, and foreclosure on real property. Foreclosure follows G.S. 105-374: an action like a mortgage foreclosure, then a public auction at the courthouse door, with a commissioner's report and a 10-day period for an increased bid. Before confirmation, the owner can redeem by paying the taxes, penalties, interest and costs.

A sale before that point is usually cleaner. The county says the first step in its advanced foreclosure process is the advertisement of the delinquent account, so an owner behind on taxes should call 252-728-8485 before the March 1 to June 30 publication window opens.

sections.h2: How does a sale affect a Carteret County tax bill?
sections.html:
Unpaid tax is a lien on the parcel, so any balance is normally cleared at closing. Ask the Tax Administration Office for a current balance before closing, and confirm with the closing attorney how the current year will be split.

The deed itself is recorded at the Register of Deeds in the same building, where the seller pays the excise tax; see our page on the Carteret County register of deeds. If a circuit breaker deferral is on the property, the deferred taxes for the preceding three years become due on a transfer.

Census QuickFacts puts Carteret County at 70,469 residents on July 1, 2025, with 54,293 housing units. The median value of an owner-occupied home was $333,300 for 2020-2024, the owner-occupied rate was 74.7%, and 30.1% of residents were 65 or older. The data is on the Census Bureau page for Carteret County.

faqs.q: What is the Carteret County property tax rate?
faqs.a: The county rate for fiscal year 2026-27 is 22.5 cents per $100 of assessed value, per the county's August 2026 news release. Towns add their own rates, and owners inside a town get one combined bill.

faqs.q: When do Carteret County taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: They become delinquent on January 6 after the September 1 due date. Anything paid through January 5 carries no interest, and after that the county charges 2% for January plus 0.75% each month.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Carteret County value?
faqs.a: For real property, 30 days from the date of the change of value notice, and for personal property, 30 days from the date printed on the tax bill. Appeals cover value only, not the rate.

faqs.q: Where do I pay my Carteret County tax bill in person?
faqs.a: Pay at the Tax Administration Office, 302 Courthouse Square in Beaufort, or the Western Office, 701 Cedar Point Blvd. in Cedar Point. Both are open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, and a drop box at the courthouse takes checks.

faqs.q: Can Carteret County set up a payment plan?
faqs.a: Yes, in limited cases. The county offers a hardship payment arrangement by application and lets owners pay in partial amounts before delinquency. A plan does not stop interest from running.
